title: TypeScript Structural and Erased
subtitle: Shape compatibility, compile-time only, runtime validation

cards.front: Two facts that define TS's type system?
cards.meaning: It is structural (compatibility by shape, not by name) and erased (types exist at compile time only; runtime is plain JavaScript). That pair explains unnamed objects satisfying interfaces, why instanceof SomeInterface is impossible, why Nest/zod validation is the runtime half of safety, and how tsc relates to Babel/SWC.

cards.front: Structural typing in TS?
cards.meaning: Two types are compatible when their members match — the needed shape is present — not because they share a declared name or inheritance relationship. Unrelated types with the same fields are often assignable.

cards.front: Is structural typing “duck typing”?
cards.meaning: At a high level yes: if it has the properties you need, it fits. That is a teaching label for shape compatibility, not a second type system.

cards.front: obj {x,y,z} assigned to Point {x,y}?
cards.meaning: OK when assigning an existing non-fresh variable — it structurally has x and y; extra z is fine. The object never had to be named Point.
cards.example: const obj = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }; logPoint(obj); // OK

cards.front: Why is TypeScript structural?
cards.meaning: JavaScript is already structural in practice: APIs care about properties and methods, not class pedigrees. TypeScript mirrors that so typing feels natural for JS, including plain objects and JSON-shaped data.

cards.front: Do named TS types create runtime brands?
cards.meaning: No. Interfaces and type names are compile-time. They do not invent runtime brands you can instanceof.

cards.front: Unrelated types with the same fields?
cards.meaning: Often assignable under structural typing. Accidental structural matches are a real consequence — two unrelated types with the same members can pass where a nominal language would refuse.

cards.front: Structural vs nominal (Java/C#)?
cards.meaning: Structural (TS): compatibility when the shape matches. Nominal (typical Java/C#): you need an explicit type relationship — extends, implements, or the same declared type. Unrelated same-shape types are often assignable in TS and not assignable nominally without casts/adapters.

cards.front: Interfaces at runtime — TS vs typical Java/C#?
cards.meaning: In TS, interfaces are erased. In typical nominal OO, types are often reflective / present at runtime.

cards.front: Can TS approximate nominal typing?
cards.meaning: Yes, with private fields or branded/unique-symbol patterns when you need intentional distinction. Advanced topic — default answer is TS is structural by default.

cards.front: logPoint({ x:1, y:2, z:3 }) error?
cards.meaning: Excess property checks on a fresh object literal — a special soundness aid on top of structural typing. z is excess when the literal is passed directly where Point is expected.
cards.example: logPoint({ x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }); // Error: z is excess on a fresh literal

cards.front: Why is extra z OK on obj but an error on a fresh literal?
cards.meaning: Variable obj already exists with its own inferred type; assigning it to Point only asks whether it has x and y. A fresh literal is checked more strictly for typos and unintended fields.
cards.notes: Mental model for this unit: structural typing plus a literal-specific guard. Full excess-property rules are the next curriculum section.

cards.front: Do excess property errors mean TS is nominal?
cards.meaning: No. They are a special check on fresh literals within a structural system, not a switch to name-based compatibility.

cards.front: What is type erasure?
cards.meaning: Type annotations, interfaces, type aliases, generic parameters as types, and most type-only constructs are removed during emit. The output is JavaScript with no type metadata — unless you use experimental/decorator emit, which still does not make interfaces runtime values.

cards.front: What does function id<T>(x: T): T emit as?
cards.meaning: Approximately function id(x) { return x; } — the generic and annotations are gone. Runtime is plain JS.
cards.example:
function id<T>(x: T): T { return x; }
// emit: function id(x) { return x; }

cards.front: Why does TypeScript erase types?
cards.meaning: TypeScript is a typed layer on JavaScript, not a separate VM. Runtime remains the JS engine you already run (Node, Hermes, browsers). Types guide the compiler and editor; they do not execute.

cards.front: value instanceof UserInterface?
cards.meaning: Impossible — interfaces and type aliases are not values. Trying value instanceof User is a compile error because User is not a value.
cards.example:
interface User { id: string; }
// value instanceof User // Error — User is not a value

cards.front: parse<T>(raw) { return JSON.parse(raw) }?
cards.meaning: No runtime checks against generic T. It lies to the type system; runtime is just JSON.parse. Generics do not enforce element types after JSON.parse or network I/O.
cards.example: function parse<T>(raw: string): T { return JSON.parse(raw); }

cards.front: When does instanceof work in TS/JS?
cards.meaning: Classes do leave runtime values — the constructor function — so instanceof checks the prototype chain vs that constructor. Type aliases and interfaces emit nothing.
cards.example:
class User { constructor(public id: string) {} }
new User('1') instanceof User; // true at runtime

cards.front: Are enums erased like interfaces?
cards.meaning: Not always. Enums may emit runtime objects depending on const enum / preserve settings. Do not lump “all TS syntax vanishes equally.”

cards.front: JS typeof vs TS typeof in type position?
cards.meaning: JS typeof checks runtime values (typeof x === 'string'). TypeScript's type-level typeof in type positions is a compile-time query of a value's type. Same keyword, different worlds.

cards.front: Runtime “is this a User?” check?
cards.meaning: Interfaces are compile-time only and fully erased — nothing to instanceof. Use classes for prototype checks, or a type predicate / zod / io-ts / Nest class-validator + DTOs for real shape checks (and optionally derive static types from the same schema).

cards.front: What is a custom type predicate for User?
cards.meaning: A function like function isUser(x: unknown): x is User { ... } that runs real JS checks and tells the checker to narrow. It is runtime logic plus a type-level claim, not a surviving interface.

cards.front: What does value-level typeof actually check?
cards.meaning: JS typeof tags. It exists because of the language runtime, not because of TS annotations.

cards.front: What does instanceof actually check?
cards.meaning: Prototype chain versus a constructor. It exists because classes/functions are values. That is why instanceof works for classes and not for interfaces.

cards.front: What does 'prop' in obj actually check?
cards.meaning: Property presence on objects. TypeScript may narrow when it sees the check; the check itself is JS.

cards.front: What does Array.isArray actually check?
cards.meaning: The runtime array brand. It is a JS check, not a TS type surviving emit.

cards.front: What do zod / class-validator actually check?
cards.meaning: Schema rules you wrote — your code or libraries. They are the runtime half of safety, not extra typing on top of interfaces.

cards.front: What does a TS type annotation check at runtime?
cards.meaning: Nothing. It is erased. Nest/zod validation is not optional extra typing — it is the runtime half of safety.

cards.front: typeof / in / instanceof — who narrows?
cards.meaning: TypeScript may narrow types when it sees these checks in control flow. That is the checker following your runtime logic, not types existing at runtime.

cards.front: tsc vs Babel/SWC on TS?
cards.meaning: tsc type-checks the program and/or emits JS (configurable). Babel/SWC transform/strip TS syntax for speed and often do not type-check. Strip is not check — a green Babel/SWC build can ship unsound assumptions if nobody ran tsc.

cards.front: What does the IDE language service do for TS?
cards.meaning: It uses TypeScript for squiggles as you type. That is editor checking, not proof that the production emit pipeline ran tsc.

cards.front: Three common tsc / bundler pipelines?
cards.meaning: 1) tsc alone — check and emit. 2) tsc --noEmit plus a bundler (SWC/esbuild/Babel) — CI/typecheck separate from fast emit. 3) Babel/SWC only — fast builds; types can be wrong until something runs tsc --noEmit.

cards.front: “We use TypeScript” — does every build type-check?
cards.meaning: Not unless CI (or the emit path) runs the checker. Erasure means a green Babel build can still ship unsound assumptions if nobody ran tsc --noEmit.

cards.front: Nest DI metadata — do interfaces survive erasure?
cards.meaning: No. emitDecoratorMetadata / reflect-metadata is extra emit, usually around classes — constructor param types as runtime hints for the container. It is not interfaces surviving as runtime values.

cards.front: Does structural typing mean no type safety?
cards.meaning: No. The program is still checked at compile time. The rule is shape compatibility, not “unchecked,” and not the same rule as nominal typing.

cards.front: Do TypeScript types exist at runtime?
cards.meaning: No, with limited enum/class exceptions for values (constructors, some enum objects). Interfaces and annotations do not.

cards.front: How does JS runtime shape-care connect to TS?
cards.meaning: JS cares about shapes at runtime; TS structural typing mirrors that at compile time. Types are then erased on emit, so runtime safety still needs JS checks or validators.

cards.front: tsc checks vs Babel/SWC strip — CI implication?
cards.meaning: tsc checks; Babel/SWC may only strip. CI must still type-check if the bundler is the emit path.

cards.front: What does type vs interface sit on?
cards.meaning: This foundation: same structural rules, different declaration tools. Excess property details continue in the next curriculum section; here you only need the seed of why people get surprised.

cards.front: Strong one-liner for structural + erased?
cards.meaning: TypeScript checks shapes at compile time and deletes those checks from the output; anything you need at runtime you must validate with real JavaScript (or a library that generates both).
